name: Can I Vibecode It?
tagline: A directory that tells you which SaaS subscriptions are one good prompt away from a personal replacement.

pricing.notes: The public directory and build prompts are free to use. The source repo is MIT-licensed.
pricing.freeTier: The public directory and prompts are free with no paid user tier.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Public directory, verdicts, prompts, alternatives and build pages.

verdictSummary: This one has receipts. The maker already published the prompt behind the site and a build page marking it as a one-shot. The core product is still pretty small: read a pile of app JSON, let people search it, render an honest verdict page, hand them a build prompt, and keep a tiny vote counter. An agent can rebuild that in one sitting. What it will not recreate in one sitting is the boring part that came after launch: the researched catalog, price checks, alternative vetting, user votes, build submissions, newsletter plumbing, and all the little production fixes. So yes, the site is vibe-codeable. The directory is the job.
coreLoopDIY: Read app JSON files, make them searchable, render a verdict page with an honest what-you-lose section and a copyable build prompt, then keep a small SQLite counter for replacement votes.
whatYouLose: The researched app catalog and the upkeep that keeps it useful
Existing votes, saved stacks, build submissions and other live community state
Fresh price checks, alternative vetting and the editorial judgment behind the verdicts
The production extras that grew around the core: newsletter delivery, auth, sponsor tooling, analytics and generated social images
moatNotes: The code is public. The hard part is accumulated editorial work and the boring production polish around it.
whyPeopleStillPay: They don't. The site is free. The reason to use the original instead of rebuilding it is simpler: cloning the software is easy; recreating and maintaining the directory is work. You can have the interface tonight. You are not getting the researched catalog, checked prices, real votes and months of cleanup with it.

priorArt.name: Can I Vibecode It? source
priorArt.desc: The MIT-licensed production repo and the proof repo behind the site's own one-shot build.

notes: The self-reference is intentional: the site already links to its own rebuild prompt in the footer.
prompt:
Build me a directory site called "Can I Vibecode It?" that answers whether a paid app is worth keeping or can be replaced with one good AI coding prompt.
Use Astro in server mode with the Node adapter, Node.js 22, better-sqlite3, vanilla JavaScript, and plain CSS. Do not add a client framework.
Keep the app catalog in data/apps/, one JSON file per app, and validate the files at build time.
Each app needs a slug, name, domain, category, price, yes/kinda/no verdict, short reasoning, what-you-lose list, moat tags, alternatives, and a copyable build prompt.
Build a homepage with fast search, category filters, verdict filters, and a ranked death list.
Show favicon, name, category, price, verdict, and replacement count in each result.
Add an app page at /<slug> with a large verdict, the reasoning, the prompt, what you lose, alternatives, related apps, and pricing details.
Add an "I replaced this" button backed by SQLite. Rate-limit it by IP and do not require an account.
Compute a collective monthly-savings ticker from app price multiplied by replacement votes.
Make search and filters work without a frontend framework.
Generate useful canonical URLs, sitemap.xml, robots.txt, structured data, and per-app social preview images.
Use a small email signup form with honeypot protection and deduplication, stored locally in SQLite.
Keep the visual direction simple: dark by default, strong monospace accents, one loud verdict color at a time, and restrained motion.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and make the site usable by keyboard.
Do not fake vote counts, prices, alternatives, or verdict confidence.
Do not add payments, sponsor tooling, social login, saved stacks, analytics, or an admin dashboard to this personal build.
Keep optional external services out of the critical path so npm install && npm run dev works with no secrets.
Add npm scripts for dev, build, start, and validate.
Write a README that explains the data format, local run, deployment, private data location, and what this build deliberately leaves out.
Finish with working code and sample app entries, run validation and the production build, and fix any failures before stopping.
